recognition.text: Ranked #37 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: This Hubble picture shows NGC 2841, a flocculent spiral galaxy about 65 million light-years away in the constellation Ursa Major. Instead of a few long, sharply defined arms, a flocculent spiral has short spiral arms, giving it a patchy, tufted look.

Star formation is one of the processes that most shape the universe. It plays a central part in how galaxies evolve, and it is during the earliest stages of a star's birth that planetary systems first appear. Even so, a lot remains unclear. Astronomers still ask how stellar nurseries change with the makeup and density of their gas, and what sets star formation going in the first place.

That second question is especially hard to answer for flocculent spirals like this one. Without long, prominent arms to point to, it is less obvious what drives new stars to form in galaxies such as NGC 2841.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.58 x 2.02 arcminutes) and distance (65 million light years), the frame spans roughly 49,000 × 38,000 light-years. Its light set out about 65 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed in ultraviolet, visible (including hydrogen-alpha) and near-infrared light. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet and near-infrared parts of this light are invisible to the human eye.
